All eight budget kinds are declared and independently enforced: source-bytes, decoded-pixels, audio-samples, video-seconds, video-frames, processor-tokens, batch and output-vectors. The product defaults are the ones the requirement states verbatim: 8 MiB and 16 megapixels for an image, 120 seconds, 32 frames and 128 MiB for video. A test asserts each number, because a default that drifts silently is a limit nobody agreed to. Budgets are enforced INDEPENDENTLY, proven by a 200-second video under the byte cap still being refused for its duration. NO SILENT SAMPLING: coverage is returned with every result, naming whether the source was fully processed, how many units were, and the sampling instruction that was applied. Incomplete coverage WITHOUT an instruction is reported as a defect rather than dressed up as policy. Decompression bombs are rejected on the DECLARED expanded size before allocation, because a check that runs after decompression has already lost. Remaining: the decoder-process bound and the actual decoded-pixel measurement are not implemented, since nothing decodes an image or video on this host; the requirement that defaults stay below the SELECTED model constraints is unenforced because no model is selected at admission time; and model context limits that may force lower admission are not consulted.

The initial per-leaf maxima are implemented and each is asserted INDIVIDUALLY - one provider attempt, no automatic repair, 60 seconds, 1024 output tokens, two image inputs - because a budget that drifts silently is a limit nobody agreed to. NARROWING ONLY EVER LOWERS: every figure takes the minimum, so a caller asking for more than the profile permits receives the profile figure. A test asserts a request for 9999 seconds yields 60. A nullable limit is narrowed the same way, and a local-only profile cannot be widened to permit remote destinations by any request. A repair is permitted only when a reviewed profile explicitly allowed one AND the same ROOT deadline still has time, because a repair consuming a fresh deadline would evade the budget rather than fit inside it. UNKNOWN COST STAYS UNKNOWN. The monetary figure has three states - a known amount, unknown with a reason - and a test asserts the unknown form contains no zero, because reporting it as zero presents a call that may be billed as free, which is the failure the requirement names. A local-only profile prohibits remote destinations INDEPENDENTLY of how the tool was implemented, since the check asks the budget rather than the implementation. Remaining: no GRANT supplies these budgets, so nothing sets model-call, token or image maxima from a server grant; the budgets are not enforced at an invocation site, only computable; and no monetary accounting is performed, so a known cost is representable but never produced.

Adjudicated (round 62, updated round 65). The native receipt is real and rich: receipt/correlation id, caller scope, parent composition id, tool/contract version, extension id/version and content digest, model identity, activation generation, durations per phase (queue/load/inference measured separately), and outcome classification (policy-denied/timed-out/cancelled/failed distinct). The run path records run receipts with real tool-call counts. External calls are wired end to end since round 63 — but as ACCOUNTINGS (timings/class/sizes), not as native provenance receipts: the two rings stay separate by design (OBS-02). Remaining: auxiliary harness-model and NESTED call receipts are not produced (no nested-call instrumentation exists), and external calls never gain a native-shaped provenance receipt (contract/implementation identity) — the accounting records the call, not its provenance.

Adjudicated (round 62, FIXED round 63, tightened round 65). The external accounting hook exists and deliberately excludes the payload (mcp/host-binding.ts:152-166,211-256), and it is WIRED: the host passes onAccounted into its own createMcpHost (bounded ring), exposes the host's OWN mcp surface as the 'model-tools.mcp-host' context service (guarded against double-mount throws, round 65), and the receipts action reports the external half with the projection declared in the output schema. ROUND 65: the round-63 review's secondary findings are fixed — the accounting receiptId now CORRELATES with the native receipt (the contract payload's meta.receiptId is used when present, so the two rings join by id; the e2e test asserts the external entry matches a native receipt) and the accounting reason is REDACTED through redactText (a raw error message can no longer carry caller content into the receipts surface). The e2e test also asserts the REAL inference result (structuredContent.language === 'de'), not merely a successful registry call. Remaining: engineVersion is recorded as 'unknown' in the wired path — the option is honest dead plumbing until the dispatch carries the serving engine's identity (recorded, not hidden); the native and external rings stay separate shapes by design; and no deployment composes startHttpServer over the service yet in this repository.

Adjudicated (round 62). The capture path is documented AND tested: the suite names every surface including the DSH LLM service this plugin cannot close, distinguishes 'we do not write here' from 'nothing is written here', states that a harness run recording nothing cannot exist, and asserts every surface this plugin writes is metadata. The metadata-only profile is tested: no bodies under either profile, residual surfaces reported, harness execution PERMITTED where no conflict and REFUSED where no-retention conflicts with reconstructability, and a non-harness tool still admitted. Remaining: the full-capture profile's body-retention behavior is described but no deployment exercises it end to end, and the headless local-specialist deployment is profile-tested without a real headless run.

Adjudicated (round 62). The diagnostics suite reports everything the requirement names: MCP on/off and endpoint, an endpointless mount as a distinct state, authorized clients, exported tools AND what was withheld, preparation status with its reason, selection, extension installation/activation state, uninstall controls, requirements, and the platform alongside the facts. An unmounted MCP surface carries the reason, an unauthenticated endpoint is reported as a risk, and UNKNOWN is its own state. Remaining: the surface is a tested report object, not rendered into a live DSH settings UI, and no test drives the settings surface from an operator's perspective.

Adjudicated (round 62, updated round 65). The measured-facts surface the requirement names does not exist: zero matches for cold-load, warm-latency, asset-size, peak-memory or correctness measurement reporting in the host. UPDATED: measured per-call timings/sizes DO now exist for external calls (the round-63 accounting ring displays totalMs/inputBytes/outputBytes with a measurement context), so 'measured-timing reporting' exists in that narrow slice — but the requirement's publishable cold/warm/asset/memory/correctness record with hardware context does not. Vendor claims and estimates are distinguished in the catalog/lock prose.

Adjudicated (round 62, subagent-verified). The host ships an EMPTY adapter registry with no special-case import, no model-name switch and no registration table, enforced by a purity gate that FAILS on a rebuilt adapter list or name switch and passes on the repo (architecture.test.ts:36-117,163-170). All FOUR model packages plus the declarative package are independent extension packages loaded through the public ./tool-mode entry.

The prohibition is now mechanically checked rather than conventional: the architecture gate rejects an extension that imports the host package by path, imports DSH, or climbs out of its own package with a relative import, and it runs over both shipped extensions as part of `npm run verify`. Both extensions import only @try-works/tool-mode-extension-sdk, with the vendor model packages reached through a dynamic import at load time rather than a static dependency. Remaining: the check covers the packages in this repository and would not see a third-party extension published elsewhere; enforcing it for those needs a packaging-time check on the consumer side.

Adjudicated (round 62, corrected per review). No built-in concept exists to follow the identical protocol: builtins.lock.json appears nowhere, BUILTIN_PROTECTED is an unused error-code string, and no protected-built-in installation or self-grant refusal exists. The five shipped packages follow one protocol because there is no alternative, not because a built-in path was built and proven identical.

Every extension is deactivatable through the same path, a built-in being a first-party package rather than an exception. Individual tools toggle independently of activation: disabling one tool leaves the package active and its other tools callable, and toggling an unknown tool is refused rather than ignored. A regression demonstrated that activation reset disabled choices; activation now restores enabled choices by tool name and excludes disabled tools plus their dependent usage skills on reactivation, while retaining unrelated tools/setup guidance. Verified state, publication and invocation admission; independent lifecycle suite 23/23. Live toggle reconciliation is now implemented: setToolEnabled is async, guarded per extension, and reconciles the PUBLISHED surface so a disabled tool and its dependent usage skill are withdrawn from the registry and a re-enabled tool is republished, with the generation advanced. Ownership is tracked separately from live handles, so a CLI attached to no host records intent without attempting to republish another process's surface. A behavioral-red registry regression now passes. Implementation-selection persistence remains incomplete. Admission now consults the committed published surface, so a tool withheld for a missing binding is not admitted from an enabled flag alone, and an unrelated unprepared deployment no longer blocks a tool whose own binding is callable; re-enabling restores admission without reactivation. Admission is now enforced AT THE CALL PATH, not just recorded: the host's extension-tool execute consults the lifecycle's admission before dispatch, so a tool whose extension was deactivated, whose withdrawal failed, or whose toggle disabled it refuses to run rather than dispatching anyway. The CLI tools enable/disable commands now take the exclusive store lock like every other offline mutation, and a behavioral-red regression proves a toggle refuses while another live process owns the store instead of racing its registry. Uninstall is implemented for third-party packages with the EXTENSION_IN_USE gate. Remaining: BUILTIN_PROTECTED is unreachable because nothing is marked built-in yet, and asset purging does not exist.

requirements.summary: One model or executor can supply several tools.
requirements.evidence: Adjudicated (round 62). Multi-tool packages are real and tested: the tongue extension declares three tools through one provider, the slice1 fixture declares three tools with three implementations, dispatch resolves each through contract to implementation, and duplicate local ids are refused at discovery. Remaining: no single package yet supplies several MODELS (the Laya multi-model example has no implementation), so the multi-model half is declared-capable but unexercised.

Adjudicated (round 62). The source vocabulary exists ('registry' | 'url' | 'local') through ONE staged install path with the same validation (archive defenses, integrity, discovery), and local archives are exercised end to end with real zips. Remaining: registry and url sources are recorded verbatim but never FETCHED (the SDK ships no fetcher; a caller injects one), so npm-exact-version and HTTPS-with-pinned-integrity installs are unproven against a real source (the same gap AT-27 names).

stagedInstall returns `activation: "inactive"` as an explicit field so a caller cannot mistake a successful install for a usable tool, and it imports nothing: the test fixture ships an entry that THROWS on import, so reaching the assertions proves installation never executed it. No inference, no warming, no tool or skill publication. Remaining: no inventory and no activation path, so the state an install produces is not yet persisted or readable.

The ordered pipeline runs and now RECORDS its result: fetch into a unique quarantine directory -> verify SHA-512 -> list entries -> validate the entry list -> extract -> discover as data -> promote by atomic rename -> record in the store lock -> remove quarantine on every path. Recording happens AFTER the bytes are in place, because a lock entry naming a directory that does not exist would make verification report a missing installation as a changed one. Remaining: dependency resolution and locking, the permission/licence/platform preview, and operator approval are not implemented.

Adjudicated (round 62). Dependency isolation is real: each version installs into an identity+version-keyed immutable directory, the runtime SDK link is made per-package to the HOST's runtime (a package-supplied copy is detected and refused — the 'pre-existing entry is not assumed to be ours' escape fix), and nothing runs npm inside the installed tree. Remaining: there is no full dependency-graph installation (transitive dependencies are not installed at all), so 'installer-owned dependency graph' covers only the SDK link.

Adjudicated (round 62). No installation scripts can run: the install path is pure archive extraction with no npm/npx/shell/exec (structural), and the AT-28 sentinel test pins it — a package with hostile install/postinstall/prepare scripts installs cleanly, the scripts land as verbatim DATA, and no sentinel appears. Remaining: the property holds because scripts have nothing to run them; no test asserts the installer would REFUSE a package whose manifest demands scripts (there is no such demand surface to refuse).

Entry-list validation refuses traversal, absolute paths, drive letters, UNC, backslashes, NUL bytes, Windows reserved device names, segments ending in a dot or space, duplicates, Windows case collisions, symlinks and hardlinks, plus entry-count, per-entry, total-byte and expansion-ratio bounds. Tested against REAL zip archives built at the byte level, because adm-zip sanitizes entry names on write and therefore cannot produce the hostile archives these defenses exist to refuse; a raw ZIP writer in the test suite supplies the bytes. The extractor re-asserts confinement at the write, so a bypassed validator still cannot escape. Remaining: fetch time limits are passed through but not enforced by the SDK, which owns no network stack.

Adjudicated (round 62). The receipt records source kind+requested verbatim, package name/version, the SHA-512 archive integrity, the content digest, and install time (install.test.ts 'leaves a receipt recording the digest and source'), and integrity mismatch is refused with advice not to retry blindly. Remaining: resolved-source, dependency-lock digest, manifest digest and permission digests are not recorded (no resolution step exists, no dependency lock exists), and re-verification on activation checks the content digest only.

discoverExtension reads package.json and the manifest as BOUNDED data (256 KB / 512 KB limits) and never imports the entry: the test fixture writes an entry that throws on import, and reaching the assertions proves it never ran. It enforces name, version, type:module, an explicit exports map, the toolMode.manifest field, containment of the manifest path, and rejects malformed or oversized JSON as INVALID_EXTENSION. Remaining: quarantine fetch, archive inspection and the install/activate lifecycle are not implemented.

extension-manifest-1.1.0.schema.json ships with the SDK and is enforced at runtime via Ajv 2020-12. Beyond the schema it checks exact id/version agreement with the package, unique local ids per contribution kind, duplicate caller-facing tool NAMES reported as TOOL_NAME_CONFLICT, referenced files that must exist, paths that must not escape the package, and unknown REQUIRED features blocking activation as INCOMPATIBLE_PROTOCOL. Unknown top-level fields are rejected while the x- vendor namespace is admitted. Remaining: asset-lock validation (EXT-15) and keyed digests.

Adjudicated (round 62). The lock-entry half is real: each assetSet resolves to a lock entry carrying provider identity, exact revision (with the kind of revision), engine/version (both disagreeing versions recorded), tokenizer/preprocessing identities, platforms, license and network behavior — tongue's is qualified, needle's is pinned with measured digests, embeddinggemma's is honestly unmeasured. Remaining: not every lock is populated (voz and embeddinggemma lack measured digests), and no validator requires every lock field before activation — a field's absence fails nothing except the qualification record.

A 1.0 manifest is normalized to module execution as a VIEW, leaving the input object untouched so the recorded digest still describes the installed bytes; the lift provenance is attached after validation rather than smuggled past the closed schema. Protocol 1.1.0, runtime API major 1, and the five separate identities are documented in code. Remaining: minor-version conformance tests and the contract/recipe/model revision separation are not implemented end to end.

requirements.summary: Publish the SDK and reference host.
requirements.evidence: The SDK now defines and exports the complete public runtime API: ToolModeExtensionV1, ExtensionContextV1, ExtensionInstanceV1, ModelProviderV1, ProviderInspectionV1, PreparedAssetMapV1, InvocationContextV1, JsonObject/JsonValue, the DisposeReason vocabulary, defineExtension() which rejects a wrong apiVersion at the declaration site, and the reserved-meta guard. Loading is implemented in load.ts: the entry is resolved from the package own exports map rather than a convention, the shape is validated BEFORE create() runs, and a missing dispose() is refused because a host with no way to release an instance could never fully stop it. Remaining: the declarative interpreter, the conformance helpers, and the reference test host with a fake harness broker are not implemented, and the SDK is not published to npm.

All five named context contracts exist with the required semantics documented: ExtensionContextV1 carries host-issued identity, private storage, a bounded logger and a teardown signal, and deliberately NO DSH ctx, registry mutation, global credentials or unfiltered environment; ProviderInspectionV1 reports readiness/features/missing/runtimeVersion and inspection is implemented to read only approved local state. The first-party inspections now distinguish readiness from residency using the full RES-04 vocabulary: a provider with all local prerequisites present but no resident model reports prepared-cold, while missing prerequisites report needs-preparation and name what to install; tests assert inspection does not load the model merely to answer readiness. Tongue's inspection is no longer mere resolvability (round 39): it stats the shipped weight bin through the package's own exports map, so a corrupted install whose bin is missing or truncated reports needs-preparation instead of publishing prepared-cold — pinned by four unit tests on the exported inspectBundledWeights verdict engine (accept complete, refuse truncated, refuse missing, refuse unresolved). Voz remains resolvability-based by design: its 367 MB weights download on first load at the model package's initiative, so no local file exists to verify at inspection time. PreparedAssetMapV1 and InvocationContextV1 carry verified handles and call-scoped grants with no caller-supplied authority. Remaining: the asset map is a type without a host implementation, and the file/network broker operations are typed but have no enforcing host behind them.

Import and create() are lightweight and tested: the extension declares no assets because Tongue bundles its weights, module import performs no work, and tests assert createProvider returns a handle in well under a second rather than parsing weights or compiling ONNX graphs. inspect() remains lightweight and read-only: it reports prepared-cold when local prerequisites resolve and still does not load the cold model merely to inspect it. Disposal is idempotent and the host disposes providers per model and instances per extension. Remaining: there is no pooling, no concurrency admission, and unload() is only a cache drop because no provider holds a process-level resource yet.

Managed extension isolation is now PRODUCTION-WIRED and independently verified (rounds 67-70). The SDK worker protocol (inspect/load/unload/invoke with a request-scoped host resolvePath broker, provider caching per model+canonical config, dispose aborting pending then unloading every provider before extension.dispose) is verified 20/20 against the built lib and the full SDK suite 296/296. The host, under the opt-in managedWorkers flag, routes ALL module-extension import/create/inspect/load/invoke through the worker (managed-workers.ts + provider-bridge.ts + index.ts): a malicious top-level entry marks only the CHILD pid, host stays alive on crashes, admission/grant enforcement refuses host-side before any spawn, generation change disposes the old worker (new pid), deactivation joins the child via the SDK onWithdrawal hook bound to workerRegistry.dispose (index.ts:2523), and default-OFF in-process behavior is unchanged. Full managed-workers suite 11/11; the full host suite 930 tests 925 pass 0 fail 5 platform skips; the full npm run verify chain passes with 1750 tests 1739 pass 0 fail 11 skips. Remaining: prepared-assets load is wired as a passthrough AND the host now HAS the prepared-asset source: the task-48 acquisition slice (plan + digest-verified acquire + prepared-cold readiness + PreparedAssetMapV1 into both provider routes) landed in round 79, and the confinement-acceptance and second-machine matrix items remain operator/external.

Adjudicated (round 62). Both contribution modes are implemented and tested: an extension may define a new tool contract (slice1 fixture's own contracts) or implement an existing one (tongue implements the standard lang-detect contract), dispatch resolves each through contract to implementation with version selection, and the two failure codes (NOT-DECLARED vs NO-IMPLEMENTATION) are distinct. Remaining: host-recognized standard contracts are recognized per-package (the manifest declares contractId), but there is no host-side standard-contract registry that independently validates a claimed standard contract — the name is trusted from the manifest.

Adjudicated (round 62). Collision rejection is real: duplicate local ids and duplicate caller-facing tool names are refused BEFORE any publication (TOOL_NAME_CONFLICT at discovery), and incompatible declarations are refused at manifest validation. Provider selection: a second implementation of a standard contract coexists by contract+version keying (the two-implementation catalog test proves two models yield one tool name), with exact-version selection over incompatible versions. Remaining: no real second implementation of one standard contract exists in the shipped packages, so 'the second implementation does not silently change the selected provider' is unit-tested, not demonstrated.

Adjudicated (round 62). Identity-bound permissions are enforced per layer: activation publishes nothing beyond the declared contributions, caller scope gates every invocation (the grant is the authority — SEC-03), enabled tools gate admission (admits requires enabled === true), the selected implementation is re-resolved per call, and an external caller's forgery of scope is refused (the invocation context is host-built). Remaining: host export policy evaluation is MCP-12's withholding only; approved profile checks exist for harness execution but no per-caller profile approval flow gates native calls.

Publication is built WHOLE and consulted before anything is registered. buildSurface produces a complete surface from the candidates, the host registers a tool only when that surface actually published it, and an incoherent surface is refused rather than partially applied. The rules EXT-24 states absolutely are enforced and tested: a tool without a runnable implementation binding is withheld (no-implementation) because a schema alone is a promise nothing can keep; a FAILED deployment is withheld with the reason that waiting will not help; an UNPREPARED model publishes readiness and a preparation skill but NOT a working inference tool; a USAGE skill is withheld unless every tool it requires is visible, naming the missing tool; duplicate tool names are REFUSED rather than silently resolved, because a name identifies one tool; and every withholding is reported with a code, subject and owner rather than dropped silently. The host now feeds the surface with extension provider inspection rather than treating every resolvable extension package as ready: ProviderBridge.inspect activates the public extension entry, creates the provider handle and calls inspect(), the control/discovery surface recomputes that read-only readiness before publication and listing, and provider-backed non-contract catalog entries are refused unless inspection reports a RES-04 callable readiness state. ProviderBridge also evicts failed activation/provider promises and is disposed on plugin teardown so inspection cannot poison an extension until restart or leak activated providers indefinitely. Skill provenance is tracked: orphanedSkills names the skills whose owning extension is gone. The TMX lifecycle also no longer publishes manifest tool contributions for model-backed contracts whose deployments are not callable: declared models default to needs-preparation until a host records a stronger readiness fact, lifecycle activation emits diagnostics, and only implementation/skill metadata is staged while the working inference tool is withheld. Remaining: the lifecycle registrar still mutates ctx.tools directly with generic schemas for callable manifest tools, so DSH tool declarations, MCP discovery and Code Mode type discovery are not yet all committed from one exact-schema generation; Code Mode type discovery still does not consume this surface.

The six dimensions are modelled separately and now PERSIST: a profile state file round-trips installation, desired and observed activation, per-deployment readiness, per-profile tool selection with the selected implementation, and export authorization independently, with profiles kept apart. A corrupt or oversized file, or one malformed entry, invalidates the whole file rather than dropping just the bad part, because a file that is demonstrably untrustworthy must not activate anything. Remaining: activation does not yet write these states, so persistence is exercised by tests rather than by a lifecycle operation.

Activation verifies the installed bytes and locks BEFORE publishing anything (a package edited after installation is refused as INTEGRITY_MISMATCH with nothing published), persists intended-active before publication so a crash leaves a record rather than a silent no-op, stages publishable contributions through an injected registrar, and commits the catalog generation ONLY once all accepted contributions have been registered. A failed registration rolls back narrowly: only the handles this activation published are withdrawn, the generation does not advance, and a healthy extension stays active AND callable - tested with one good and one failing package in the same profile. Readiness is assessed rather than assumed: declared models default to needs-preparation until prepared readiness is recorded, unprepared model-backed tools are withheld with diagnostics instead of advertised as working inference, and a FAILED deployment refuses activation because it will not become ready by waiting. Contract-version regression tests first demonstrated false publication and wrong-version dispatch; lifecycle now withholds a tool when the available bindings implement only another contract version, and dispatch selects an exact contract ID/version match regardless of candidate order. Activation-time usage skills resolve required local tool IDs and remain withheld when those tools are withheld; setup guidance remains visible. Publication now checks readiness of the first exact-version binding, matching dispatch selection; a cold-first/ready-second regression demonstrated false visibility before the fix and now withholds both tool and usage skill. Persisted readiness is projected onto currently declared deployment IDs: removed failures no longer poison activation, while failures for current deployments still refuse activation without publication (behavioral-red regression and complementary fail-closed test, independently verified). Tools with no implementation or no exact-version implementation are now withheld, and admission requires the committed published tool set, not just an enabled state flag; complementary regressions assert no-implementation admission is false and unrelated unprepared models do not make a model-free tool inadmissible. Readiness now has a PRODUCTION WRITER: ExtensionLifecycle.recordReadiness records host-inspected deployment readiness (dropping deployments the current manifest no longer declares), and the host restore path inspects every provider-backed catalog entry of the extension being restored and records the results before activation. Recording is guarded per extension and RECONCILES the surface when readiness actually changed, so a deployment that just failed has its published tool withdrawn and one that just became callable is published — the published snapshot can no longer go stale in either direction. Regressions cover publish-after-record, withdraw-after-downgrade, and unknown-extension/unreadable-manifest refusal. Adversarial review then closed three further gaps: inspection failures now record `failed` instead of carrying a stale prepared state; readiness is keyed by the manifest model id rather than the catalog entry id; and the byte-integrity gate now runs BEFORE inspection imports any extension code. EXACT-SCHEMA publication now covers the extension-contribution path too (round 36): the host registrar reads each contributed tool's MANIFEST-declared input/output schemas from the installed copy (bounded at 512 KB, degraded with a log rather than failing other tools), projects them through the same DECL-02 projection, and derives output closedness from the declared schema instead of hardcoding it. A host-restore regression asserts the manifest's `token`/`upper` types and requiredness reach the real registry. Projection review follow-ups also landed: nested array `items` are now advertised (the old strip was stale against the pinned registry and a stricter-than-contract bug in waiting for any field NAMED items), non-scalar enums are dropped in projectNode's post-pass for both input and output paths, annotation-only nodes project to `type:'json'` instead of crashing registration, and enum keywords inside annotation DATA pass through untouched. Remaining: the extension path's dropped-keyword enforcement is now real — assertAgainstSchema validates both arguments and results against the DECLARED manifest schemas at the call path, with a regression proving a 300-char token is refused against the declared maxLength 256 that the projected advertisement drops. Extensions WITHOUT catalog rows are inspectable via ProviderBridge.inspectExtension (store-copy resolution, bounded timeout), so embeddinggemma/needle readiness is a recorded fact rather than a permanent default; no managed worker is started and the public entry/API is not validated, because there is no worker runtime; provider handles are not created. A declared schema the host cannot read or compile now REFUSES the tool instead of publishing it unenforced (round 40, P26-13): the throw reaches the lifecycle, whose narrow rollback withdraws only this extension's handles and quarantines it with the reason named, and a regression proves a valid-JSON-but-invalid-schema package installs cleanly, fails restore, and its tool never reaches the registry.

Deactivation persists inactive intent before withdrawing, withdraws contributions, and refuses to claim a full stop when it cannot confirm one. A NEW CASE was found while writing the CLI tests: a fresh process (or a CLI not attached to the host) holds no publication handles, so it cannot withdraw another process's contributions. It previously reported a clean stop in that situation, which is the exact lie EXT-27 forbids. The lifecycle now detects an extension recorded as active while this instance holds no handles and reports the cleanup failure with guidance to stop the owning host, leaving the state quarantined. Withdrawal failure now retains lifecycle handles and host-registrar name ownership until disposal succeeds, allowing explicit cleanup retry; two behavioral-red regressions now pass and independent review verified 36 focused tests. Uninstall now refuses incomplete deactivation and retains installed records/quarantine; quarantine and crash-interrupted deactivating states without local handles remain unverified across retries instead of falsely reporting a full stop. Behavioral-red uninstall/orphan regressions pass, and a review-found deactivating crash gap was repaired with additional regression coverage. Activation rollback now retains failed withdrawals and quarantines surviving contributions without advancing generation. Reactivation is refused when local handles or quarantine/interrupted activation/deactivation remain; interrupted activation without local handles cannot establish a clean stop. Cross-kind same-name contribution handles are indexed independently so rollback cannot collapse them (review-found regression). Per-extension same-instance exclusion now rejects overlapping activate/deactivate/uninstall/toggle operations across asynchronous publication/withdrawal; a deferred-publication behavioral-red regression now passes and the guard releases on settlement. Durable ownership closes the cross-process case: state records the publishing PID (stamped on active/activating, stripped on a confirmed stop), so a restarted process restores an `active` extension whose owner died (dead-PID regression) while a LIVE second owner is refused, and the same process cannot adopt its own foreign instance. Reconcile now applies the activation integrity gate and refuses rather than wiping when the manifest cannot be read, keys contributions by kind and name, and treats a redundant toggle as a no-op without advancing the generation. Remaining: cross-instance/process lifecycle ownership is not serialized, explicit verified recovery of dead-owner quarantine is absent, active calls are not cancelled, disposal hooks are not called, no grace period is joined, and no owned process is terminated, because there is no worker runtime.

Uninstalling an active package returns EXTENSION_IN_USE unless deactivation is explicitly requested, and the CLI now prints the impact preview (affected profile and each contributed tool) before refusing, as EXT-28 requires. With --deactivate the deactivation sequence runs first; the record is removed only after fullyStopped is confirmed (a fresh CLI without owning publication handles now refuses instead of erasing quarantine), the disabled tombstone is RETAINED so nothing silently resurrects the package, and --purge-assets reports that deletion may complete after restart on Windows. Remaining: private resolved dependencies are not deleted, credential references and executable-content approvals are not revoked, and BUILTIN_PROTECTED is not reachable because nothing is marked built-in.

Adjudicated (round 62). Cleanup discipline is real: uninstall keeps a tombstone, crash-mid-deactivation is refused rather than half-removed, failed rollback handles are retained until cleanup succeeds, quarantine is reported rather than a clean stop, purge deletes only unreferenced content-addressed assets, and the CLI reports 'asset purge requested' where Windows deletion may complete after restart. Remaining: no native-library/model-file release is awaited (no in-process native libs exist to release), and no retry-on-restart cleanup flow executes owned deletion — the tombstone records the request, but nothing retries it.

EXT-30 IMPLEMENTED (rounds 63-78, independently re-verified gates 5-7). Invocation receipts and lifecycle records exist as SEPARATE structures, because mixing them would let a caller reading a receipt learn about operator actions it has no business seeing and would make an audit trail indistinguishable from execution metadata. A receipt records the extension package, its version, the content digest, the dependency-lock digest, the model/recipe identity, the activation generation and the execution location; the content digest is what lets two runs of the SAME version be told apart, since a package can be replaced at one version. Receipts are emitted on every SUCCESSFUL call and NOT on a refused one, because a receipt for a call that failed validation would claim provenance for a result nobody received; verified through the real pipeline, including that the invoked text never appears in a receipt. The metadata-only rule is enforced by CONSTRUCTION: buildInvocationReceipt takes only host-resolved inputs, so there is no parameter through which a body, token or skill text could arrive, and every warning passes a redactor that strips npm/GitHub/bearer tokens and absolute paths of either shape. redactPath reduces a path to its leaf plus a short digest, so an operator can correlate two receipts without learning the filesystem layout. Lifecycle records carry the operation, outcome, profile and approving principal, refuse an operator approval with no identity, and carry no execution fields. The log policy defaults to quiet, metadata-only, telemetry off, and REFUSES an undeclared network origin rather than logging it. Remaining: receipts are retained in a bounded in-memory ring, not persisted to a receipt store; lifecycle records are built but not yet emitted by the CLI or the lifecycle; the store still records no dependency-lock digest, so that field is always null; and extension logging is not yet driven through the policy by a real extension.

Subscription ids are the LISTEN REQUEST IDs per the pinned schema (corrected round 59 — the earlier 'server-issued' reading described an older design; the identification follows the request that opened the subscription, and isolation comes from the per-client binding, not from caller-chosen ids, which would let one client address another subscription), and closing one requires ownership. TEARDOWN IS ANNOUNCED: revoking a grant sends notifications/cancelled referencing the SUBSCRIPTION REQUEST before the subscription is removed, so a client learns its access ended rather than inferring it from a dropped stream, and there is no window in which one last event reaches a revoked client. Revoking one client leaves unrelated clients alive. P26-10 is respected by omission: the catalog stream emits only notifications/tools/list_changed, never progress or logging, which belong on the response stream of the call that produced them. Remaining: there is no SSE response stream, so a subscription is a series of messages on the request response channel rather than a long-lived event stream; resource and prompt catalog changes do not exist, so only toolsListChanged is supported and advertised.

The channel separation rule is respected and tested: the catalog subscription stream emits ONLY notifications/tools/list_changed, never progress and never logging. Progress stays on the response stream of the call that produced it, because routing it onto the catalog stream would deliver one call progress to every subscriber. Protocol logging is not adopted at all, which the revision deprecates, so there is no logging channel to conflate with model-facing results. Remaining: there is no request-scoped SSE response stream, so progress cannot actually be delivered on an originating call stream yet - the separation holds because neither channel exists rather than because two exist and are kept apart, and interleaved subscriptions with active inference calls on one client are therefore not exercised.

Adjudicated (round 62, subagent-verified). The advertised-feature matrix declares sampling/elicitation/roots implemented:false (mcp/protocol.ts:211-230) and serverCapabilities derives ONLY from that matrix (mcp/server.ts:359-367), so nothing unsupported is advertised — tested at three levels (mcp-protocol.test.ts:332-348, mcp-server.test.ts:180-187, mcp-live-schema.test.ts:283). No server-originated JSON-RPC requests are emitted anywhere (the dispatch returns only responses plus revision-defined notifications, mcp/server.ts:126-246), so the MRTR pattern has no surface to violate. The earlier NOT_RUN reading missed that the requirement's operative clause is 'nothing unsupported is advertised', which is fully implemented and tested.

Optional extensions are not conflated with ordinary tools: the advertised-feature matrix declares tasks, sampling and elicitation as NOT implemented, and P26-12's rule is enforced by a test that reads the matrix. THE MATRIX WAS ALSO CORRECTED: subscriptions/listen was declared implemented unconditionally while the only production transport received no registry and answered -32601, so a client could plan around a feature it could never obtain. The feature is now re-decided from the WIRING and defaults to false, and a client REQUIRING it receives -32021 rather than a capability it cannot use.

The JSON Schema 2020-12 baseline is supported, and published contracts plus actual inputs and outputs are validated against it; unsupported dialects and constraints are REJECTED rather than silently accepted. The pinned schema is the authority (`docs/tool-mode/specs/mcp-2026-07-28/schema.json`) and the saved-fixture probe validates 39 recorded messages against it. PARTIAL for a reason worth stating plainly: the live server's own messages are validated by the unit and live suites, but the probe that checks recorded fixtures NEVER STARTS THE SERVER, and no live response is currently Ajv-validated against the pinned definitions end to end — the gap that let the -32021 data shape through.

The revision declared TTL/cache-scope mechanism is used: cacheable results carry cacheScope private and ttlMs 0, which the pinned CacheableResult definition REQUIRES on DiscoverResult and ListToolsResult alike, asserted by test and by schema validation. Zero TTL with a private scope is the correct default for an authorization-filtered catalog: a shared cache keyed on tool names would leak one caller permitted set to another. Remaining: nothing caches yet, so the fields state the policy rather than govern a cache; authorization is not recomputed per invocation at the MCP boundary because the caller-permitted set is not yet computed there.

The OAuth 2.1 resource-server profile is now IMPLEMENTED over an embedded local authorization server (round 43), alongside the static-token mode which remains custom authentication that claims nothing. The embedded server is the P26-15-permitted second option and the crypto boundary it draws is respected: signing and verification use Node's own WebCrypto HMAC-SHA256, and only the JWT envelope is assembled here — no cipher or hash is hand-rolled. What is verified: HS256 credentials with iss/sub/aud/scope/iat/exp/jti; signature-first verification (a tampered payload is refused before any claim is read); issuer, audience and expiry validation with leeway; scope validation with RFC 6750 insufficient_scope challenges naming the required scope; per-client credentials with INDEPENDENT revocation (one client's revocation leaves a peer client's token valid, at the verifier and at the HTTP layer); RFC 8414 authorization-server metadata and RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata served unauthenticated at the well-known paths; and the transport answers invalid_request/invalid_token/insufficient_scope challenges with the matching error codes. The live scheme is reported per deployment: authProfile() and claimsOAuthConformance() now take the auth configuration, so a static-token host still reports oauth21ResourceServer false. Remaining: no dynamic client registration (not a prerequisite — clients are pre-registered, which P26-16 explicitly permits), no refresh tokens, and the profile is proven at the handler level, not yet wired as the default for a live server binding.

Tested here: origin rejection, invalid and missing tokens, mixed clients with independent credentials, token leakage (a failure response is asserted not to contain either the configured token or the presented one), and header/version errors. With the OAuth profile landed (round 43), the previously-missing cases now exist and are pinned: expired tokens, wrong audience, wrong issuer, tampered signatures, insufficient scope (with the required scope named in the RFC 6750 challenge), per-client independent revocation at both the verifier and the HTTP layer, and the metadata endpoints served unauthenticated. Remaining: bridge credential protection is untested because the bridge does not exist, and headless operation fails with actionable guidance for a missing token but no interactive approval path exists.

A fixture corpus and a SEPARATELY AUTHORED PROBE exist. Each records what it demonstrates and the expectation an auditor can check. The probe (scripts/probe-mcp-conformance.mjs) is independent by construction: it reads the frozen files from disk, imports none of the server, dispatch or protocol modules, and validates against the PINNED upstream schema with Ajv, so it cannot inherit a mistake from the code that produced the fixtures. It runs in npm run verify and reports 39 checks with 0 failures (the MANIFEST's probeCheckCount, mechanically maintained by the probe itself since round 59 — the earlier '34 checks' was stale). The manifest pins the schema by immutable commit and records the official SDK version: the v1 line cannot speak this revision, while the v2 line implements it via discovery (qualified round 57), which is part of the MCP-04 answer. The probe found FOUR real defects on first run: two fixtures that LIED about what they demonstrated (a loopback-refusal case captured from the loopback address, and a domain-failure case that used an unpublished tool name so it recorded an invalid-params error instead), a JSON-RPC error carrying id null which the pinned RequestId type does not admit, and a mapping bug in the probe itself. What it does NOT establish is stated in the probe header: the fixtures were produced by this repository own code, so the probe shows the CAPTURED BYTES satisfy the upstream definitions, not that every possible request would. Remaining: subscription and SSE fixtures are absent because those surfaces do not exist, and the selected-SDK half of the requirement cannot be met while the v2 packages are not installed on this machine — this is an adaptation, so there is no independent SDK side to cross-check against here.

verification/requirements.json now exists and maps every normative ID to its owning module, test layer, required platform, source digest and evidence, generated from the pinned spec text rather than maintained by hand, so a requirement cannot silently go missing. requirements.summary: Install the built tarball into a clean compatible DSH installation on Windows without source symlinks, TypeScript loaders or compiler toolchains.

requirements.summary: Start with no optional weights, no cloud credentials and no browser. Diagnostics work; discovery downloads nothing; unavailable tools are not falsely advertised.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 55). Startup is READ-ONLY by policy and by test: RUN-05 permits only restoring an approved activation and inspecting local state, and REFUSES preparation, resolution and downloads at startup, with the prohibition encoded in the policy type (server-lifecycle.test.ts). Discovery downloads nothing: the SDK has no network stack (its only fetcher is injected), and the host's acquisition path is operator-approved and separate from discovery. Unavailable tools are not falsely advertised: the extension inspection reports unprepared with reasons, MOD-20's data-level SUPPORTED_PART_KINDS restricts advertised inputs, the live server reports an unknown tool as an error, and resource governance refuses unprepared/unavailable deployments rather than admitting them. Diagnostics work: OBS-04's suite reports MCP state, authorized clients, withheld tools, preparation status with its reason, and the platform. Remaining: 'no cloud credentials' is structural (nothing reads any) rather than tested; 'no browser' is the no-DOM architecture (no test attempts one); and the whole chain is not exercised in ONE cold-boot test with assertions on zero network and zero weights.

requirements.summary: The embedded MCP server starts/stops with plugin configuration; port conflict, malformed config and restart behave predictably.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 55). The server lifecycle is tested through its states: readiness only after bind AND initialise both succeed; a failed initialise closes the bound listener; a failed start does not throw and cannot crash the host; a PORT_IN_USE conflict is REPORTED with a remedy that rules out force and stealth and does NOT return a port (nothing can silently relocate); a second start is refused rather than binding twice; shutdown refuses new work, cancels owned work, terminates what outlives the grace period, and releases the port (a second server can bind it — mcp-live-conformance); stopping an already-stopped server is a no-op; and disabling the server does not disable unrelated DSH tools (RUN-01). Restart behaves predictably through the same start/stop paths. Remaining: 'starts/stops with plugin configuration' is exercised via the test harness's configuration object, not a real DSH plugin-profile config round-trip, and malformed-config behavior is tested through initialise failure rather than a config-schema rejection at the boundary.

requirements.summary: A genuine 2026-07-28 reference client and an independent protocol probe/client both discover and invoke tools using the modern wire contract. Record SDK/client versions; a legacy Inspector alone does not prove modern support.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 55, corrected round 57). The independent probe/clients exist and run: mcp-live-conformance drives the LIVE server over a real socket (discover, tools/list, tools/call with real inference, credential refusals, header mismatches) and probe-mcp-conformance validates 39 checks over 17 recorded fixtures against the PINNED 2026-07-28 schema. The GENUINE reference client EXISTS and supports the revision — the v2 line of @modelcontextprotocol (server/client/core 2.3.1) implements 2026-07-28 via discovery, and this repository's own MANIFEST.json records officialSdkSupportsRevision:true with the interop suite (6 tests, 0 skipped at capture time) — but the packages are NOT INSTALLED on this machine, so the v2-interop suite is SKIPPED here: an environment absence, not an upstream impossibility (the round-55 review's correction). Remaining: a genuine reference client invocation has not been re-run on this host since the packages left node_modules, and the modern era remains opt-in upstream (the v2 client's default still negotiates the legacy handshake).

requirements.summary: Two simultaneous clients share a model pool but cannot read each other's files, credentials, receipts or execution state.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 55). Concurrent clients are served without interleaving (mcp-live-conformance: two concurrent calls with id-correlated answers), and per-client isolation is tested at the strongest available point: OAuth revocation of ONE client leaves a peer client working, and a revoked credential is refused at the HTTP layer. The model pool is shared by construction (one host registry, one extension store). Remaining: the two-client MCP test uses ONE credential identity, so two INDEPENDENTLY credentialed clients sharing the pool is untested; and 'cannot read each other's files/receipts/execution state' is structural (the MCP surface exposes no file or receipt tools, and receipts are per-invocation) rather than adversarially attempted.

requirements.summary: A stdio-only reference client reaches the same server through the bridge without starting a second inference host; stdout remains protocol-clean.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 55). The bridge is the stdio adapter and is tested at protocol level: it generates the modern headers (version from the BODY, Mcp-Name only when the body names a tool), posts to the CONFIGURED endpoint — the same server an HTTP client reaches, so no second inference host is started by the bridge — forwards bodies verbatim with request ids preserved, cancels per-request, aborts everything it owns on EOF, and keeps stdout protocol-clean (a success writes exactly one protocol frame and no diagnostic; diagnostics go to the diagnostic channel). Remaining: no genuine stdio-only reference client binary drives the bridge end to end; the tests drive the bridge adapter directly.

requirements.summary: Authorized Native and MCP calls have equivalent semantic values and contract schemas, excluding call IDs/timing.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 56). The schema-equivalence half is enforced: MCP-08/MCP-09 tests assert every published tool's output schema is DERIVED from the contract (only the reserved meta property removed, the remaining constraints preserved verbatim, the contract not mutated), a host success that violates the advertised output schema is rejected, and the tool_mode_run MCP projection conforms to the PINNED schema before shipping. MCP calls go through the same host invocation path as native calls (one dispatch authority is also a verify:architecture gate). Remaining: no test runs the SAME tool through Native and MCP side by side and diffs the semantic values excluding ids/timing — the equivalence is asserted per-layer, not by a value-level diff.

requirements.summary: The unchanged leaf tools work in DSH PTC and return usable structured fields, not prose to be parsed.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 56). The leaf tools DO work in DSH PTC: ptc-composition.test.ts runs REAL programs on the real NodePtcRuntime — a program that calls TWO tools, branches on a DEPENDENCY, and returns canonical output; the other branch; abort; ungranted-tool failure; tool failures surfaced through the program. The structured-fields half is the composition contract: the run output is a ToolModeRunOutput with a structured result, and the runtime's output ledger bounds serialized JSON. Remaining: the composition exercises the fixture tools, not the REAL unchanged leaf tools (lang_detect etc.) — the unchanged-leaf-tools-in-PTC half is untested end to end; and the tongue/lang_detect native path predates the PTC slice.

requirements.summary: External `tool_mode_run` performs the local-only transcription/decision composition with real outputs and zero harness-LLM requests; separately performs the title/image harness composition with explicitly counted and authorized auxiliary requests.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 56). The gate and the accounting halves exist: tool_mode_run is REGISTERED and refuses without the operator grant (CODE-10 default) and refuses even with the grant while confinement is undemonstrated (CODE-09); the exposure gate reports its state and reason from one enforcement point; the served path reports result, logs, elapsedMs and REAL tool-call counts (the binding counter wraps every bound call). Zero harness-LLM requests is structural: the backend is the local PTC runtime, and no code path in the run pipeline calls a harness model. Remaining: the local-only transcription/decision composition cannot run (its tools are the voz/tongue/Laya set, of which Laya is BLOCKED upstream), the title/image harness composition with counted authorized auxiliary requests is not implemented (the broker exists with a journal sink, but no composition uses it in the acceptance sense), and the gate stays CLOSED in production by design, so no external tool_mode_run has ever executed.

requirements.summary: Generated loops and branching work; independent calls obey both program and cross-client provider limits.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 56). Loops and branching DO work: ptc-composition runs a program that branches on a dependency and returns canonical output through the real runtime. Independent calls obey the PROGRAM budget: the deadline is clamped (a null or oversized request cannot widen it), and cancellation aborts exactly the referenced request. Remaining: no test drives an actual GENERATED loop (the composition programs are hand-written), no cross-client provider-limit test exists (the two-concurrent-clients MCP test is one identity), and the runtime revision has no explicit nested-call depth bound.

requirements.summary: An injected invalid output and invalid nested field fail validation through every surface; denied/rewritten canonical results cannot leak through `structuredContent` or PTC.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 57, corrected round 59). Injected invalid output fails validation through the SURFACES THAT EXIST: the host output check refuses a provider result violating its own declared output schema (host-restore.test.ts: the __violate_output__ fixture manufactures a number where the schema declares a string, and the HOST check is the one refusing — the fixture performs NO output check itself, so the matched message can only come from the host's assertAgainstSchema); the MCP binding rejects a host success whose structured value violates the advertised output schema; the DSH projection is never stricter than the contract (nullable unions, scalar enums, null-valued members all admitted); a successful MCP call carries schema-valid structuredContent and a bounded text rendering; and the registry's projection drops unsupported constraints from the ADVERTISEMENT while the call path still enforces them (maxLength enforced at the call path, asserted against the HOST check). Nested-field validation is asserted at the schema layer (contracts.test.ts 'refuses a nested field violation'). Remaining: no end-to-end test drives ONE invalid output through Native + MCP + structuredContent + PTC in sequence and asserts refusal at each; the PTC path's output validation is the runtime's output ledger, not the contract schema.

requirements.summary: Missing/invalid token, hostile Origin/Host, ungranted tool, excessive body and rate-limit tests fail before inference.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 55, RATE-LIMIT HALF BUILT round 66). Each named refusal is tested: missing credential, wrong token and non-Bearer scheme refused on EVERY request including discovery (mcp-http); hostile Origin refused (including an unapproved origin that looks local) with CORS never treated as authentication; hostile Host refused even on loopback; ungranted tool refused by the grant authority (SEC-03: the grant is the authority, not the request); excessive body — the size limits exist in the SEC-02 method/path/size suite. All of these fail BEFORE inference: the auth and authority layers precede dispatch in the request pipeline. THE RATE LIMITER NOW EXISTS (round 66): a per-client fixed-window limiter keyed on the AUTHENTICATED identity (static-token clientId / OAuth subject — never the socket address), enforced BY DEFAULT (60 req/60 s, operator-overridable, false = explicit off), placed AFTER auth and BEFORE body parsing, refusing with HTTP 429 + Retry-After and a schema-pinned JSON-RPC error using the documented implementation-defined code -32001 (the pinned revision defines no rate-limit error; the reserved band was not touched). 13 tests cover exhaustion, boundary reset, per-client independence, config validation, bounded idle eviction, the pinned-schema envelope, default/off overrides, and the no-auth-oracle rule (auth failures never consume budget). Remaining: the limiter is fixed-window (bursts at boundary edges are possible), in-memory per host instance (no cross-instance quota), and the adversarial 'excessive body AND rate-limit combined' scenario is tested through separate suites rather than one combined run.

requirements.summary: Windows traversal, absolute-path escape, junction/symlink escape, device/UNC paths and unauthorized artifact/receipt IDs are refused. Include Unicode and space-containing valid paths.

evidence.evidence: Windows traversal, absolute-path escape, junction escape, device/UNC paths and unauthorized roots are all refused, with Unicode and space-containing valid paths admitted (authority.test.ts, real filesystem). Remaining: the artifact/receipt identifier half of the test — the checklist requires that UNAUTHORIZED artifact/receipt IDs are refused, and while a bounded in-memory receipt ring now exists (MAX_RETAINED_RECEIPTS, receipts view; corrected round 57 — the earlier 'no receipt store exists' wording was stale), no test drives an unauthorized identifier at the store.

requirements.summary: Hosted code cannot read forbidden files/environment, open unapproved network destinations, import prohibited modules, spawn unauthorized processes or access management bindings. Test attempts, not only configured flags.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 55, corrected round 57). The confinement is tested with ATTEMPTS, not flags: ptc-sandbox runs real programs against the real sandbox and the read-only mode REFUSES a write the program attempts, with the ENFORCEMENT the sandbox actually applied reported back (the workspace-write mode cannot start in this Windows environment — ACL grant fails — and is skipped, which the suite reports honestly). Management bindings are refused by the CODE-07 excluded set even when granted and visible, and prototype/reserved-name bindings are rejected with a null-prototype non-writable map. Network destinations require explicit authorization (SEC-10). CORRECTED: imports are NOT prohibited in the runtime — the program body runs through new AsyncFunction and the runtime documents that Node APIs are available through await import(...); confinement is enforced at the SANDBOX layer (filesystem/network/subprocess ACLs), not at import. Remaining: the workspace-write attempts are skipped on this host, and spawn/prohibited-module confinement is covered by the sandbox ACL layer rather than by driving a hostile program at each prohibition end to end.

requirements.summary: Infinite loops, overlong inference, oversized logs/results, too many nested calls and cancellation terminate or settle within declared bounds and leave no uncontrolled child processes.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 55, citation corrected round 57). The bounds exist and are enforced at the runtime: the deadline is clamped (a null or oversized request cannot widen it), the wall timer aborts on expiry and the managed child is TERMINATED with waitForExit awaited before the outcome settles, and the server lifecycle terminates work that outlives the grace period and reports it. Cancellation is classified as cancelled, never as a failure (RES-06: the abort outcome maps to 'cancelled', distinct from 'failed'). Output is bounded by the runtime's output-ledger with overflow reported as a limit outcome rather than dropped silently. Remaining: infinite-loop termination is the deadline mechanism (no loop detector), 'too many nested calls' has no explicit depth bound in this runtime revision, and oversized-logs/results bounds are tested at the unit level rather than by driving a hostile program at each bound end to end.

requirements.summary: Disabling a tool or revoking a client stops new and queued admissions; subsequent discovery updates. A captured composition binding does not bypass revocation.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 55). The stop-and-update halves are implemented at the authoritative points: disabling a tool makes admissions refuse it (resource governance + lifecycle admits checks), deactivation withdraws every published contribution and admissions refuse the extension's tools, and discovery is LIVE — tools/list advertises the registry as it is at request time (mcp-live-conformance), so a subsequent discovery reflects the change. Client revocation is per-client and immediate: a revoked credential is refused at the HTTP layer, and a peer client keeps working. The captured-binding half is the strongest part: the PTC authority re-reads the visible set at RUN time (index.ts 'Read at RUN time, not once'), so a composition captured before a deactivation is refused when it runs. Remaining: no admission QUEUE exists to stop queued items (admission is synchronous), and no end-to-end test captures a binding, disables the tool, and runs the program.

requirements.summary: Changing an interactive agent to PTC does not break MCP direct calls; parallel clients never toggle a global presentation mode.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 56). The non-interference half is structural and partially tested: MCP direct calls go through the host path independent of any Code-Mode state (the MCP surface is derived from the registry, which PTC mounting does not mutate — the mount is GUARDED in both directions and never overrides an existing provider), and parallel MCP clients are served without interleaving. requirements.summary: Deactivate built-in and third-party packages during queued/active calls. Subsequent calls and captured bindings are denied, skills/types update, resources settle, and unrelated clients/extensions remain usable.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 53). Remaining: no built-in package concept exists (nothing to deactivate), no worker runtime exists to show resources settling mid-call, and 'queued/active calls' at deactivation time are untested because the admission path has no real queue.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 52). Version coexistence is structural: installation directories are keyed by identity AND version (install.test.ts), and installing the same version twice is refused. Duplicate caller-facing tool names are refused at discovery with TOOL_NAME_CONFLICT (sdk.test.ts), so two implementations of one standard tool cannot both publish under one name. requirements.summary: A package cannot steal a tool/skill name, self-mark as built-in, inherit another publisher's grants or gain access by reusing a URL/name/version. Permission/identity changes require approval.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 53). Name stealing is refused: TOOL_NAME_CONFLICT at discovery (sdk.test.ts), duplicate local ids refused, and identity is exact — the manifest id must equal the package name and the version must equal the package version (sdk.test.ts), so a package cannot reuse another's URL/name/version to claim its surface. Self-marking as built-in has no path: BASE-09's architecture tests scan the host sources and reject any rebuilt built-in adapter list (architecture.test.ts), and the activation policy vocabulary admits only operator or bundled-default — no extension-declared built-in status. Inheriting another publisher's grants has no path: grants are host-issued, and SEC-03's authority tests prove the grant is the authority, not the request. Remaining: there is no permission/identity-approval FLOW to require approval (nothing changes permission at runtime, so nothing asks), and no test drives a hostile package at the whole-pipeline level (the refusals are asserted per-layer).

requirements.summary: Failed activation and failed updates roll back catalog publication. Successful side-by-side updates preserve old callers' semantics or fail them explicitly; rollback preserves revocations/disabled state.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 53). Failed-activation rollback is real and heavily tested: a failing publication withdraws the contributions THIS call published and leaves the generation where it was; interrupted activation is refused rather than overwritten; failed rollback handles are retained and reactivation is refused until cleanup succeeds; a crash left mid-deactivation is refused rather than half-removed. Disabled state survives the rollback paths by construction (state writes carry the persisted enabled flags). Remaining: no update flow exists at all (there is no migration from a prior format — the same gap as AT-18), so side-by-side updates, old-caller semantics and rollback-preserves-revocations are untestable.

requirements.summary: Windows native-worker/file locks, interrupted transactions and crash recovery produce truthful cleanup-pending state and eventual owned cleanup. Shared assets/profiles are not deleted or killed by another owner's uninstall.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 57). The interrupted-transaction half is real: crash-mid-operation states are refused rather than half-removed (deactivation intent without local handles refused; interrupted activation refused rather than overwritten; failed rollback handles retained until cleanup succeeds), cleanup-pending is reported as quarantine rather than a clean stop, and the restart path restores only what the operator approved. Cross-owner protection is structural and tested: the store lock refuses a live foreign holder and treats a dead holder as stale, assets are content-addressed with purge deleting only unreferenced bytes, and the shutdown path NEVER touches work owned by another still-authorized owner. Remaining: Windows native-worker file locks are untested (no native worker exists to hold a file lock), and 'eventual owned cleanup' has no retry-driven cleanup flow — the quarantine is a reported state, not a scheduled cleanup.

requirements.summary: Throwing/hung extension callbacks and malformed worker messages cannot crash the DSH host. Adversarial fixtures test actual confinement guarantees; an explicitly approved trusted-code exception must not claim protection from malicious unconstrained native code or bypass generated-Code-Mode confineme…

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 57). The crash-isolation halves are implemented at the dispatch boundary: an extension failure PROPAGATES as a tool failure rather than returning an empty success, a failed dispatch produces NO execute function at all, the provider is resolved per call so a deactivated extension is never served from a stale handle, a hung cleanup is quarantined rather than reported clean, and a refusal is readable with a remedy. Malformed messages are answered on the PROTOCOL channel as errors (stdio: a malformed frame is answered, not swallowed; the wire layer rejects malformed requests with -32602). Remaining: no adversarial fixture throws or hangs INSIDE the extension worker process and proves the host survives (the callbacks are in-process, and there is no managed worker process for them to run in); the 'trusted-code exception must not claim protection from malicious native code' clause is honored only vacuously — no trusted-code exception exists.

requirements.summary: An ordinary MCP client/program cannot install, activate, update, remove packages or change exports. Cross-client metadata, secrets and grants remain isolated after catalog changes.

evidence.evidence: Adjudicated (round 57). The cannot-manage half is structural at every boundary: the MCP surface exports EXACTLY the tools the host registered (no install/activate/update/remove tools exist in the registry — those are CLI commands, never tools), the composition surface REFUSES the management and composition bindings (tool_mode_run, model_tools, tool_mode_list, tool_mode_describe) even when granted and visible, and MCP-12 withholds tools that cannot be exported faithfully rather than partly exporting them. Cross-client isolation: per-client OAuth grants and revocation are independent, and a tools/list reflects the registry at request time. Remaining: no test drives an ordinary MCP client AT the install/activate commands and asserts refusal (the surface simply lacks them — a missing-surface guarantee rather than a refusal test), and 'change exports' has no export mechanism to change.

requirements.summary: Run the complete independent-author scenario through Native, MCP and hosted composition. Archive the built package, protocol/schema version, Windows/runtime evidence and lifecycle results as release artifacts.

THE SCENARIO NOW RUNS as scripts/e2e-orchestration.mjs (verify:orchestration): packed install into a clean project (host in place + workspace tarballs + DSH closure), default preparation (listing/describe), TWO MCP clients over a real socket (authenticated static-token client gets 200 tools/list + a REAL lang_detect through tools/call; unauthenticated gets 401), lifecycle round-trip (disable withdraws and refuses, enable restores real inference), receipts evidence, and honest SKIPPED stages with reasons (title tool needs a harness provider offline; hosted composition needs a PTC program in the packed closure).
